The foundational principle of cybernetics centers on the quantification of information within noisy communication channels. Carrier telephony enables multiplexing by separating signals in frequency domain, increasing line efficiency. The core insight is that information capacity is bounded by Shannon-Hartley theorem, which depends on signal-to-noise ratio and bandwidth. Noise introduces uncertainty, limiting reliable transmission. Thus, information content is inversely proportional to randomness—haphazard sequences carry no information, while structured ones do. This leads to a duality: regularity measures information, whereas irregularity denotes entropy. The failure mode arises when noise overwhelms signal strength, rendering channel unusable. Temporal regularity becomes critical in modeling sequential data, enabling prediction and control in feedback systems.
